prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)  -- More than half the Christian population has fled the northern Iraqi city of Mosul in reaction to a campaign of killings and intimidation, according to the United Nations. Christian women attend a religious service Sunday at a church in Baghdad. An estimated 13,000 Christians have left because of oppression the U.S. government blames on al Qaeda in Iraq. Mosul, in Nineveh province, is one of the last Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq has a significant presence and routinely carries out attacks. An estimated 2,300 families have fled Mosul this month, but the exodus has started to ebb, Nineveh province's Deputy Gov. Khasro Goran said Tuesday. No Christian family has left the city over the past seven days, and at least 100 families returned to their homes in and around Mosul during that time, Goran said. Authorities said they believe Christian demonstrations earlier this month may have prompted the attacks. Hundreds of Christians took to the streets in Mosul and surrounding villages and towns demanding adequate representation on provincial councils, whose members will be chosen in local elections in January. The violence that followed those protests left at least 14 Iraqi Christians dead and prompted the Iraqi government to dispatch more security forces to patrol the city. Violence has declined as a result, Iraqi officials said. Last week, U.S. Defense Department spokesman Geoff Morrell said the anti-Christian attacks and threats are partly "due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there." "This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups," Morrell said. The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees is helping many of the displaced families, most of whom have fled to nearby villages in Nineveh province. About 400 others have crossed into Syria, but many have said they no longer feel safe there, according to the refugee agency. Syria already hosts more than 1 million Iraqi refugees. The U.N. agency said many of the Iraqi Christians told stories of intimidation and death threats. "One woman said she and her mother left Mosul early last week, two days after someone called one of her colleagues at work and said that all Christians should leave the city immediately or be killed," according to a UNHCR news release. "She said she was unnerved but decided to leave only after hearing reports that 11 people had been killed at a checkpoint by militiamen dressed as police officers. She and her mother escaped with a couple of bags and all the money that they had in the house -- they did not dare go to the bank to remove their savings." A nurse told UNHCR that the threats against Christians in Mosul began months ago "with phone calls, letters and messages left on doors." In other violence Tuesday in Mosul, four police officers were killed and four wounded when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle, an Iraqi Interior Ministry official said. Gunmen in cars ambushed police as they were on their way to start work in west Mosul's al-Amil neighborhood, the official said. Also Tuesday in Baghdad, six civilians died and 23 were hurt in four bombings, the official said. In eastern Baghdad, in the Shiite al-Baladiyat neighborhood, a roadside bomb exploded Tuesday afternoon, killing one civilian and wounding five others, the official said. Earlier, a parked car exploded near a busy outdoor market in the western al-Jihad neighborhood, killing at least five people and wounding 11 others, the Interior Ministry official said. No other details were available about the blast. Two roadside bombs exploded in central Baghdad's al-Nahdha commercial area, wounding seven people, the official said. The first blast hurt four civilians, while the second wounded three, the official said. Also Tuesday, the Iraqi army and police discovered 20 decomposed bodies in the basement of an abandoned house in Tal Afar, a town about 43 miles (70 kilometers) west of Mosul. There was no indication of how the victims -- who could not immediately be identified -- were killed, the official said. Authorities discovered the bodies after receiving tips from local residents. CNN's Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) —** More than half of the Christian population has fled the northern Iraqi city of Mosul in response to a campaign of killings and intimidation, according to the United Nations.

Christian women attended a religious service Sunday at a church in Baghdad.

An estimated 13,000 Christians have left Mosul because of persecution that the U.S. government attributes to al Qaeda in Iraq. Mosul, located in Nineveh province, is one of the last Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq maintains a significant presence and routinely carries out attacks.

An estimated 2,300 families have fled Mosul this month, although the exodus has begun to subside, Nineveh province Deputy Gov. Khasro Goran said Tuesday. No Christian family has left the city over the past seven days, while at least 100 families have returned to their homes in and around Mosul during that period, Goran said.

Authorities said they believe Christian demonstrations earlier this month may have prompted the attacks. Hundreds of Christians took to the streets in Mosul and surrounding villages and towns to demand adequate representation on provincial councils, whose members will be selected in local elections in January.

The violence that followed the protests left at least 14 Iraqi Christians dead and prompted the Iraqi government to deploy additional security forces to patrol the city. Iraqi officials said violence has declined as a result.

Last week, U.S. Defense Department spokesman Geoff Morrell said the anti-Christian attacks and threats were partly “due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there.”

“This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups,” Morrell said.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees is assisting many of the displaced families, most of whom have fled to nearby villages in Nineveh province. About 400 others have crossed into Syria, although many have said they no longer feel safe there, according to the refugee agency. Syria already hosts more than 1 million Iraqi refugees.

The U.N. agency said many Iraqi Christians had recounted experiences of intimidation and death threats.

“One woman said she and her mother left Mosul early last week, two days after someone called one of her colleagues at work and said that all Christians should leave the city immediately or be killed,” a UNHCR news release said.

“She said she was unnerved but decided to leave only after hearing reports that 11 people had been killed at a checkpoint by militiamen dressed as police officers. She and her mother escaped with a couple of bags and all the money that they had in the house — they did not dare go to the bank to remove their savings.”

A nurse told UNHCR that threats against Christians in Mosul had begun months earlier “with phone calls, letters and messages left on doors.”

In other violence Tuesday in Mosul, four police officers were killed and four others wounded when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle, an Iraqi Interior Ministry official said. Gunmen traveling in cars ambushed the officers as they made their way to work in the al-Amil neighborhood of western Mosul, the official said.

Also Tuesday in Baghdad, six civilians were killed and 23 others injured in four bombings, according to the official.

In the Shiite al-Baladiyat neighborhood of eastern Baghdad, a roadside bomb exploded Tuesday afternoon, killing one civilian and wounding five others, the official said.

Earlier, a parked car exploded near a busy outdoor market in the western al-Jihad neighborhood, killing at least five people and wounding 11 others, the Interior Ministry official said. No further details about the blast were available.

Two roadside bombs also exploded in central Baghdad’s al-Nahdha commercial district, wounding seven people, the official said. The first blast injured four civilians, while the second wounded three.

Also Tuesday, the Iraqi army and police discovered 20 decomposed bodies in the basement of an abandoned house in Tal Afar, a town about 43 miles (70 kilometers) west of Mosul.

There was no indication of how the victims, who could not immediately be identified, had been killed, the official said. Authorities discovered the bodies after receiving tips from local residents.

outputs.L2:
**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) —** A wave of murders and threats has driven more than half of Mosul’s Christian community from the northern Iraqi city, the United Nations reported.

Christian women attended Sunday worship at a Baghdad church as an estimated 13,000 Christians left Mosul amid persecution that the U.S. government has attributed to al Qaeda in Iraq.

Located in Nineveh province, Mosul remains among the few Iraqi cities where al Qaeda in Iraq maintains a substantial presence and regularly launches attacks.

Nineveh Deputy Governor Khasro Goran said Tuesday that approximately 2,300 families had departed Mosul during the month, although the flow of people leaving had begun to slow. According to Goran, no Christian families had fled in the previous seven days, while at least 100 families had returned to residences in Mosul and nearby areas.

Officials said demonstrations by Christians earlier in the month may have triggered the violence. Hundreds of Christians protested in Mosul and neighboring towns and villages, calling for sufficient representation on provincial councils whose members were to be selected in January’s local elections.

At least 14 Iraqi Christians were killed in the violence that followed the protests. In response, Iraq’s government sent additional security personnel to patrol Mosul. Iraqi authorities said the increased security presence had helped reduce the violence.

The previous week, U.S. Defense Department spokesman Geoff Morrell said the threats and assaults targeting Christians were partly “due to elements of al Qaeda that still enjoy some ability to operate up there.”

“This is an attempt, it appears, to try to inflame tensions and fault lines that exist between religious and sectarian groups,” Morrell said.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has been assisting many of those displaced. Most escaped to villages elsewhere in Nineveh province. Roughly 400 traveled across the border into Syria, though many told the refugee agency that they no longer considered Syria safe. The country was already sheltering more than 1 million Iraqi refugees.

According to the U.N. agency, numerous Iraqi Christians described receiving threats and being subjected to intimidation.

A UNHCR statement recounted the experience of one woman who fled Mosul with her mother early the previous week. They left two days after one of the woman’s co-workers received a telephone call warning that every Christian must immediately leave the city or face death.

The woman said the call frightened her, but she did not decide to flee until reports emerged that militiamen dressed as police officers had killed 11 people at a checkpoint. She and her mother took only several bags and whatever cash was inside their home. They were too afraid to visit the bank and withdraw their savings.

A nurse also told UNHCR that intimidation of Mosul’s Christians had started months earlier through telephone calls, letters and messages placed on doors.

Elsewhere in Mosul on Tuesday, gunmen attacked a police vehicle, killing four officers and injuring four more, according to an Iraqi Interior Ministry official. The attackers, traveling in cars, ambushed the officers as they headed to begin their shifts in the al-Amil district of western Mosul.

Four separate bomb attacks in Baghdad that same day killed six civilians and wounded 23, the official said.

In al-Baladiyat, a Shiite neighborhood in eastern Baghdad, a roadside bomb detonated Tuesday afternoon. One civilian died and five others were injured.

Earlier, a parked vehicle exploded near a crowded open-air market in the western al-Jihad district, leaving at least five people dead and 11 wounded, the Interior Ministry official said. No further information about that explosion was immediately available.

Two additional roadside bombs went off in the al-Nahdha business district in central Baghdad. The first injured four civilians, and the second wounded three.

Also on Tuesday, Iraqi soldiers and police found 20 decomposing bodies in the basement of an empty house in Tal Afar, approximately 43 miles, or 70 kilometers, west of Mosul.

The victims could not immediately be identified, and there was no indication of how they had died, the official said. Authorities located the remains after area residents provided information.

CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to the report.

More than half of Mosul’s Christian population—an estimated 13,000 people—fled the northern Iraqi city after a wave of killings, threats, and intimidation. Iraqi officials and residents blamed at least some of the violence on al Qaeda in Iraq, saying Christian families had been targeted in an apparent effort to drive them from their homes.

The sudden exodus prompted the Iraqi government to increase security patrols in Christian neighborhoods and around churches. Additional checkpoints were established, while police and military units stepped up their presence in an effort to reassure residents and prevent further attacks. The United Nations also began assisting displaced families, many of whom sought refuge with relatives or in predominantly Christian towns and villages outside Mosul.

Recent developments suggest that the immediate crisis may be easing. No Christian families were reported to have left Mosul during the past week, while at least 100 families returned to the city. The decline in departures and the first significant wave of returns indicate that residents may be gaining confidence in the improved security measures.

Nevertheless, the situation remains fragile. Sectarian tensions persist, and thousands of Christians remain displaced and uncertain about whether it is safe to return permanently. Continued protection, humanitarian assistance, and efforts to address the groups responsible for the intimidation will be necessary before Mosul’s Christian community can fully recover.

counterfactuals.output:
# Mosul’s Christians Driven From Their Homes by Killings, Threats and Fear

**MOSUL, Iraq — October 2008** — A campaign of killings and intimidation has forced thousands of Christians to flee Mosul, deepening fears that one of Iraq’s oldest religious communities is being systematically pushed out of the northern city.

Christian residents have described gunmen targeting people near their homes and workplaces, while threatening messages and rumors of further attacks have spread through predominantly Christian neighborhoods. Families have sought refuge in villages north and east of Mosul, often arriving with few possessions and uncertain prospects of returning.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, or UNHCR, reported that roughly **2,200 Christian families — about 13,000 people — had fled Mosul during the first weeks of October**. UNHCR accounts said displaced families reported receiving threatening telephone calls, text messages and written warnings ordering them to leave. Some said attackers had marked or identified Christian homes.

The agency cautioned that displacement figures were changing rapidly as families moved between Mosul, nearby Christian towns and relatives’ homes. Earlier UNHCR counts were lower, reflecting the pace of the exodus and the difficulty of registering people scattered across numerous communities.

Khasro Goran, the deputy governor of Nineveh province, characterized the violence as an organized campaign against Christians rather than a series of unrelated crimes. He said Christians had been singled out in targeted shootings and that attacks on homes had added to the pressure on families to flee.

Goran and other local officials warned that the campaign appeared intended to alter Mosul’s demographic balance. The city and the surrounding Nineveh Plain have long been home to Chaldean Catholics, Assyrians, Syriac Catholics and other Christian communities whose roots in the region predate Islam.

Casualty figures varied among agencies because some reports covered different periods. The **Iraqi Interior Ministry reported that at least 11 Christians had been killed in a series of attacks beginning in late September**, while provincial officials and subsequent accounts put the toll higher, at approximately 12 to 14. The victims included shopkeepers, laborers and other civilians attacked because of their apparent religious identity.

The killings followed years of pressure on Iraq’s Christian minority. Churches in Baghdad and Mosul have been bombed, clergy members have been kidnapped or murdered, and families have faced demands to convert, pay protection money or leave. In March 2008, the body of Archbishop Paulos Faraj Rahho, the Chaldean Catholic archbishop of Mosul, was found after he was abducted following a church service.

Iraqi authorities deployed additional police and soldiers to Christian districts and established checkpoints around churches and neighborhoods. The government also announced investigations and offered financial assistance to displaced families. Christian leaders, however, said the measures would matter only if authorities identified those responsible and could guarantee residents’ safety over the long term.

In Washington, Pentagon spokesman **Geoff Morrell** said the attacks appeared to be coordinated and acknowledged concern about the displacement of Mosul’s Christian population. At the same time, he said U.S. officials had not reached a definitive conclusion about who was directing the campaign. American and Iraqi officials considered several possible perpetrators, including al-Qaeda in Iraq, local criminal groups and factions seeking political or territorial advantage in Nineveh.

Morrell also addressed allegations that members of Iraqi security units might have been involved or had failed to intervene. He said the United States had not seen conclusive evidence establishing official participation, while emphasizing that the accusations required investigation.

Responsibility remained contested. Some Iraqi officials blamed Sunni extremists seeking to restore sectarian conflict as security improved elsewhere in the country. Others pointed to political rivalry over control of Nineveh and the disputed territories surrounding Mosul, where Kurdish, Arab and minority parties were competing for influence ahead of provincial elections.

That uncertainty intensified fear among displaced Christians. UNHCR accounts described families sheltering in churches, public buildings and overcrowded homes in places such as Bartella, Qaraqosh, Tel Kaif and other towns on the Nineveh Plain. Host communities and religious organizations supplied food, blankets and emergency cash, but aid workers warned that local resources were being stretched.

Many of those who fled said they had left behind businesses, schools and property. Some departed within hours of hearing about a nearby killing or receiving a warning. Others sent women and children away first while male relatives remained to guard homes or close shops.

The displacement has consequences beyond the immediate humanitarian emergency. Iraq’s Christian population, estimated at more than one million before the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, had already declined sharply because of emigration and internal displacement. Community leaders warned that another sustained exodus from Mosul could further erode a religious presence that has survived in northern Mesopotamia for nearly two millennia.

Although security deployments later encouraged some families to consider returning, UNHCR said returns had to be voluntary and based on credible guarantees of safety. For many displaced residents, checkpoints and official assurances were not enough.

The central question was whether the killings would be investigated and prosecuted. Until those behind the campaign were identified, Christian families said, returning to Mosul would mean going back to neighborhoods where threats could reappear at any time — and where religious identity itself had become a potential death sentence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
